prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and its realisation, with many atoms interrogated at once, at a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: After the full first round my preferred configuration is unchanged: B029 as the whole prize, credited to Katori and Ye. Four of the eight round-1 configurations contain it with the identical pair, and the four members who prefer other candidates all list it as an acceptable fallback; that counts for nothing by itself, but it does tell me the scientific record is not in dispute, only its weight. What I rely on is the measurement evidence. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) report systematic uncertainty and stability near 1e-18 and agree in direct frequency-ratio comparisons, so the claim does not depend on one group's error budget. Katori's magic-wavelength scheme is what makes a many-atom ensemble usable without lattice light shifts, and Ye's work took it into the quantum-projection-noise-beating, many-body regime and to the quoted accuracy. The consequence I weigh most as an experimentalist is that the instrument now measures something about nature: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tight limits on drifts of constants and on dark-matter couplings. I accept Danielsson's point that the citation should rest on demonstrated performance and not on the redefinition of the second or on geodesy, which are prospects. My proposed citation therefore names the lattice scheme and the 1e-18 realisation, which meets the chair's question of how to word it so that the comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes are not implicitly re-awarded.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is that a measurement advance is not a new behaviour of matter, and that the 2005 and 2012 prizes paid for the ruler and for single-ion control; Eriksson and Mehlig press this and it is a legitimate reading of what a physics prize is for. A second objection is attribution at the edges: Lemonde, Peik and Hollberg on the proposal side, and Ludlow, Bloom, Lemke, Hinkley, Kitagawa and the ion-clock groups on the achievement side, are real contributors, and the best ion clocks still compete on accuracy. As the chair asks, I do not think these change the two-name set: Katori is the originator of the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and Ye's group is the one that carried it to 1e-18 across both the systematics and the many-body regime, and the named others fit as team members or as parallel refinements. The record cannot fully dissolve the proposal-history question, so I would accept an outside check of the 2001-2003 priority documents before a final ranking. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet occurred.

responses.point: Eriksson defends B031 as prediction followed by decisive experiment, separates the established discovery of correlated and superconducting phases from the open pairing mechanism, and asks the experimentalists whether superconductivity has been seen in enough independent samples and groups. He also rates B029 as a refinement of precision spectroscopy rather than a new behaviour of matter.
responses.response: You asked the experimentalists about reproducibility, and I accept that the phases themselves have been seen by several groups, so I withdraw part of my round-1 objection: the open mechanism is a footnote to the discovery and not a reason to defer. What still concerns me is that you yourself say twist-angle disorder decides which phases appear in a given device, so a statement such as 'reproduced' needs qualifying in a way that 1e-18 comparisons between independent clocks does not. The credit is also not settled: if the committee takes the prediction-plus-experiment pair you accepted for Olsson, I would regard B031 as much more defensible than with Bistritzer plus an omitted Cao and Dean group, and your answer that you cannot resolve this from the supplied names is the main reason I keep it second. On novelty, I disagree that the clock is only a refinement: going from a single ion to a million-atom lattice at the magic wavelength is a different route past the quantum-projection-noise limit, and it is what allows a gravitational potential to be resolved across a bench. That does not make B031 a lesser result; it is a different kind of prize, and I would list it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig calls the lattice clock a refinement of the ruler created by the 2005 and 2012 prizes, ranks it second, and says the cleaner credit set alone should not decide between B029 and B031. He also notes that the transparent analytic flat-band mechanism makes B031 an understood discovery at single-particle level.
responses.response: I agree that a clean credit set should not decide the question by itself, and I do not want it to; the case must be scientific. I would answer 'refinement of the ruler' with a distinction: the comb gave a means of counting optical cycles and Wineland's methods gave control of one ion, but neither produced the lattice-clock architecture, in which the magic wavelength cancels the trap shift to the level that lets thousands of atoms act together. A quantity that improved by orders of magnitude and then changed what could be observed, such as redshifts over millimetres, is for me a discovery in measurement and not only a tidy-up. I do accept your analytic-mechanism argument for B031 and I find it persuasive for the flat-band picture; my remaining hesitation is the many-body ground state and the age of the field. If the committee wants a statement of new matter, you have made the better case for that than I expected, and that is why B031 now stands as my first alternative instead of B004 or B001.

responses.point: Lindroth wants the citation limited to the lattice scheme so the whole of optical clocks is not claimed, and, in answering the chair, is the colleague asked to confirm with me that the proposal-history and ion-clock questions leave the two names unchanged.
responses.response: I confirm the two-name set from my own reading of the field, and I am glad that we now agree the wording should be anchored on the lattice scheme. Where we still differ slightly is emphasis: I would keep the realisation at 1e-18 in the citation, because the magic-wavelength idea alone was published years before the clocks reached that regime, and the Nobel Committee has tended to reward demonstrated achievement. I do not think the ion-clock groups create a credit problem, since their approach is a different physical route and is already covered by the 2012 prize. I also accept your caution that benefits should not be over-stated, and I would not cite the redefinition of the second.

responses.point: Johansson prefers circuit QED (B004) with Blais, Schoelkopf and Wallraff, and has flagged a possible recusal on that candidate and deferred to the chair.
responses.response: I appreciate that you flagged your closeness to B004 and I think stepping back from the ballot on it is the cleaner course, and I would hold myself to the same standard on the WACQT overlap I disclosed. On the science I still regard circuit QED as original and reproduced, and that is why it remains one of my alternatives. My worry is not the physics but the sequence after the 2025 prize on circuits, and the four-names-for-three problem, which the record does not settle: your choice to drop Girvin differs from my opening ballot, which kept him and dropped Blais. A committee that cannot agree on the three should not rank it above a pair that all colleagues independently name.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes a two-part prize, B029 with Katori and Ye plus a single-laureate B037 for IceCube (Francis Halzen), arguing that precision metrology and a new astronomical messenger are two distinct achievements within three names.
responses.response: I agree on the B029 part and on resting it on demonstrated performance, but I would not add B037 to it. I see no scientific kinship between the two parts, and the three-name limit is a reason to be selective, not a reason to pair. A sole credit to Halzen for an observatory collaboration, with the AMANDA precursor and others, is the part you concede is weakest, and that weakness would damage the clock half in the public eye. If the committee prefers two parts, I would sooner discuss it again, but I would not support a configuration whose second part rests on the attribution you describe.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 2005 and 2012 prizes as having covered enough of optical precision measurement that a lattice-clock prize is not distinct enough.
Whether an outside assessment of the 2001-2003 proposal history (Katori, Lemonde, Peik, Hollberg) would alter the credit between proposal and realisation.
Whether to await the formal redefinition of the second; I do not treat it as a condition, but I cannot say what the committee will accept.
Whether the credit for B031 should be two or three names and how the omission of Cao, Fatemi and Dean's group would be explained, since that decides how I rank my first alternative.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I spent a year of my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is a 2005 laureate for the frequency comb. He is not a credited name in B029, and I have no tie to Katori, Ye or their groups, but my closeness to the laser-spectroscopy community should be recorded. My work on rare-earth-ion crystals and quantum memories is adjacent to B004 and B001. As the chair asked, my WACQT leadership role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, where Goran Johansson works, so I would step back from any decisive ballot on B004 and I do not rank it as a lead. I see no other conflict.
